title: Giving attention
hook: the most common gift is simply listening

segments.voice: Yesterday, samvibhaga, if people knew: if beings saw the fruit of giving, they'd share even the last bite. Your line was share the last bite.

When did someone last really listen to you? Not nodding while typing. Not waiting for their turn. Really listening: phone somewhere else, eyes on you, a question that showed they'd heard. For some people the answer is a name and a day, weeks back. This week is about dana, giving, and so far it's been food and things. But there's a gift almost nobody counts as a gift, and it costs nothing except the one thing people are shortest on. Attention.
screen: `WHO REALLY LISTENED TO YOU?` → `A NAME, WEEKS BACK.` → `A GIFT THAT COSTS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, honesty about the sources. The old lists of gifts in the Pali texts talk about food, drink, clothing, shelter, lamps, medicine, and above all the gift of the teaching. They don't have a sermon titled listening is giving. But they come very close. In one discourse, the Buddha describes the gift of a good person, and the list starts not with what you give but how. A good person gives with faith, gives respectfully, gives at the right time, gives with a generous heart, and gives without harming anyone. That word, respectfully, sakkacca in Pali, means with care, with attention, with your whole self in it. A bowl of rice tossed carelessly and a bowl of rice offered with care are not the same gift. The attention is part of what's given. Another list names four ways that hold a community together: giving, kind speech, helpful action, and treating people as equals. Three of the four are about how you are with people, not what you hand them. Put those together and you arrive where some Buddhist teachers today arrive: attention is a gift. Anyone can give it. Nobody can give it while doing something else. And it has a strange property: when you give someone your full attention, you get to be fully somewhere yourself. It's the practice from the cushion, the breath, the feet, turned toward a person: the same steady noticing, pointed at someone's face instead of your own breath.
screen: `THE OLD LISTS: FOOD, LAMPS, TEACHING.` · `SAKKACCA: GIVING WITH CARE.` · `FOUR THINGS THAT HOLD PEOPLE TOGETHER.` · `THE CUSHION, TURNED TOWARD A PERSON.` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Give your full attention to the sounds around you, one at a time, the way you'd listen to a friend, without naming or judging them. Then bring to mind one person you'll see today, and picture sitting with them, phone away, eyes on them, listening all the way to the end of their sentence before you answer. Notice how it feels even to imagine it.
Giving attention. The gift of full presence: listening with care, the way the texts say a good person gives, respectfully.
Your line: attention is a gift. Anyone can give it, and nobody can give it halfway. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers describe attentive listening as a form of generosity, and the texts praise giving 'respectfully', with care, as part of what makes any gift a good one.

guess: the gift of full, caring presence

fork.setup: a friend starts telling you something hard. your phone buzzes on the table. what does today's teaching point toward?
options: check it quickly; you can listen at the same time.
turn the phone face down and listen to the end.
fork.reveal: the gift here is attention, given with care, the way the texts praise giving respectfully; it can't be given halfway.

original.note: Pali: respectfully, carefully, with attention; the texts praise giving sakkacca, with care.

trapdoor: what you thought: giving means money or things.
what it means: attention is a gift, and care is part of every gift.
what a scholar hears: AN 5.148 lists the good person's gift as given with faith, respectfully (sakkacca), at the right time, generously and without harm; AN 4.32 gives the four sangaha-vatthu.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.148 (Sappurisadana Sutta), the gift of a good person
Anguttara Nikaya 4.32 (Sangaha Sutta), four ways of holding people together

notes: The script says plainly that the Pali texts don't name listening as a form of dana; the framing that 'attention is a gift' is presented as what many teachers today say.
The five qualities of the good person's gift are paraphrased from AN 5.148; confirm the list and the reference.
The four sangaha-vatthu (giving, kind speech, helpful conduct, impartiality/equal treatment) are paraphrased from AN 4.32; confirm.
